Introduction
Among population-based metaheuristics whose mechanisms are modeled on collective animal behavior, algorithms inspired by group hunting occupy a distinct niche. The best-known example — the Grey Wolf Optimizer (
GWO
) — is based on a simple hierarchy: the entire pack moves toward the three best individuals, and each wolf follows the same strategy. The
Chimp Optimization Algorithm (ChOA)
, proposed by Khishe and Mosavi in 2020, superficially resembles this scheme but is based on a different idea — the
heterogeneity
of intelligence within the group.
Chimpanzees live in a fission-fusion society, where the composition and size of hunting groups are constantly changing, and where hunting success depends not on uniformity but on the division of roles. The authors of the algorithm identify four types of individuals with different abilities and strategies: drivers follow the prey and pressure it without attacking; barriers block escape routes, trapping the prey; chasers quickly catch up with the prey, causing panic; and, finally, attackers anticipate the escape route and finish the hunt. In optimization terms, these four roles are assigned to the four best solutions in the population, and the remaining individuals update their positions based on all four leaders at once, rather than on a single leader. It is precisely this heterogeneity — the different laws governing changes in coefficients for different groups — that distinguishes ChOA from the homogeneous GWO family.
The second pillar of the algorithm is what the authors refer to as social motivation. In addition to rational pursuit of prey, chimpanzees tend to exhibit impulsive, chaotic behavior — a drive to obtain meat at any cost for subsequent social exchange. In the mathematical model, this translates into a chaotic component: with a certain probability, an individual updates its position not according to the hunting formulas, but by a jump determined by a chaotic map. The purpose of this mechanism is to enable the algorithm to escape from local optima to which a smooth collective search inevitably converges.
Mathematically, ChOA can be described concisely. Each individual's position is recalculated as the average of four candidate positions. Each candidate is drawn toward its leader using a distance distorted by random and chaotic coefficients. The dynamic coefficient, which determines the balance between exploration and exploitation, decreases monotonically over the course of the iterations: at the beginning, the steps are large and the population explores the space extensively; by the end, it converges toward the leaders it has found. The chaotic replacement described above operates on top of this.
ChOA is, by its very nature, continuous. However, many applied problems require a binary solution. A classic example
is
feature selection in machine learning, where a subset must be chosen from thousands of features, and the solution is encoded as a bit string indicating
included/excluded
. In 2023, Ayeche and Alti closed this gap by proposing Enhanced Binary Chimp (BChimp): they took the ChOA core and added a binarization layer in two variants — BChimp1 (stochastic crossover of four binary steps) and BChimp2 (a sigmoid transfer function). It is this work that we use as our basis — the specific coefficient curves and the algorithm's formulation itself are taken from it.
However, our ranking covers continuous optimization, so we remove the binarization layer, revealing the same continuous core beneath it — in terms of its mechanism, this corresponds to the original ChOA, bringing us full circle. Naming convention in this article: we retain the name BChimp for the implementation, after the specific work we reproduce and test, and use ChOA when referring to the continuous predecessor that provided the core.
In this article, we will implement the algorithm using the standard C_AO framework. We will run it through the usual set of test functions (Hilly, Forest, Megacity) at different dimensionalities and assess its position in the shared ranking. Along the way, we'll need to carefully compare the code with the publication and the original source. We will also need to correct an inherited coefficient defect that goes unnoticed in a binary problem but destroys the search in a continuous one — and, in the process, uncover hidden characteristics of the algorithm that distort its evaluation on the usual tests.

Figure 1. Two Position Update Modes in ChOA
The left panel shows the hunting phase.
Individual X(t) (gray) repositions itself using the four leaders surrounding the prey as reference points: the attacker, the barrier, the chaser, and the driver. For each leader, a candidate (X1…X4) is calculated — an attraction along the corresponding direction with its own role coefficients. The new position X(t+1) (green) is the average of the four candidates — the center of gravity of the attractions, pulling the population toward the best solutions.
The right panel shows the chaotic phase.
With a probability of 0.5, a regular update is replaced by a jump: the individual’s coordinates are replaced by the value of a chaotic map (the gray dots show how the chaotic sequence covers the search space). It is precisely this phase that has been omitted from our continuous implementation.

Coordinate-wise randomness.
The coefficients a_k and c_k are resampled for each coordinate j; each agent has its own chaotic multiplier m[i]. Even though m[i] is the same for all of the agent’s coordinates, the coordinate-wise variation is provided by a_k and c_k — therefore, a shared scalar that confines a candidate to a subspace does not arise, and there is no diagonal advantage on a symmetric benchmark.
Symmetric a.
The factor f·C1G_k specifies the step amplitude and decays to zero by the end of the run, while the factor (2·rand − 1) makes the step symmetric (mean zero). This corrects the defect discussed in the description section: in the published form, the random component is shifted away from zero, causing the population to drift into a corner in continuous search.
Elitism.
Each of the four leaders stores its best-ever position, rather than the best position in the current population; the population itself moves freely, without rollback.
The chaotic replacement phase of the original ChOA (where a position is replaced by a chaotic value with a probability of 0.5) has been omitted: in the continuous problem, it proved to be detrimental to convergence. For a binary problem (feature selection), line 20 is replaced by a binarization step — either sigmoid thresholding of the mean (BChimp2) or crossover of four binary steps (BChimp1).
Let's move on to the implementation.
The C_AO_BChimp class inherits from the base class C_AO and follows the framework's standard life cycle: the Moving method proposes new positions, the outer loop evaluates fitness, and the Revision method updates the best positions. All internal state beyond that of the base agent is stored in structures — this keeps the data for the four leaders and the individual state of each agent self-contained, without flat buffers (index × coordinate).
The four leaders are stored as an array called lead[4] (0 = attacker, 1 = barrier, 2 = chaser, 3 = driver). Each leader is self-contained, and working with it does not require manually recalculating offsets in the shared buffer.
In addition, the class maintains the iteration counters epochs, epochsDen, and epochNow for the t/T ratio, as well as a single visible parameter, popSize.

Init begins with StandardInit, which sets up the search boundaries and the array of agents. The initial population is then randomly distributed into cP[] — on the first call to Moving, it will be copied to the working coordinates c[] so that the outer loop can evaluate it. The four leaders are initialized with a fitness of -DBL_MAX, representing empty slots that will be filled during the first revision.
A separate block precomputes the chaotic multiplier based on the Piecewise map (index 6, P = 0.4, initial value x0 = 0.7). The value is taken
before
the next map update.
Each agent receives its own static multiplier m[i], which is the same for all its coordinates and remains unchanged throughout the run — exactly as in the original implementation.
The epochsDen counter is set to epochs − 1: this ensures that the ratio t/T reaches one precisely on the last actual iteration, and the control multiplier f = 2 − 2·t/T correctly decays to zero by the end of the run.

The first call is special: while 'revision' is still 'false', the method simply transfers the starting coordinates from cP[] to c[] using the SeInDiSp projection (clamping to the boundaries while accounting for the step size) and exits, handing control back to the outer loop for the first evaluation.
On subsequent iterations, the epoch coefficients are recalculated first: the ratio tRatio = epochNow / epochsDen, the shared multiplier aCoef = 2 − 2·tRatio, and the group curves using the cube-root law u1 = (t/T)^{1/3} and the cubic law u3 = (t/T)^3 (arrays C1G, C2G). Next, for each agent and each coordinate, four candidates are generated — one per leader — and averaged.
The key detail is the form of Ak: the group curve C1G[k] serves as the amplitude, while randomness is introduced through a symmetric multiplier (2·rand − 1) with zero mean. This is precisely what corrects the inherited bias: in the published formulation, the random component was shifted, causing the population to drift toward a corner in continuous search space. Random values of Ak and Ck are drawn anew for each coordinate, so despite the scalar m[i], there is no shared multiplier for the entire vector, and the algorithm gains no geometric diagonal advantage.

Revision first updates the personal (fB, cB for each agent) and global (fB, cB) best solutions. Next, InsertLeader is called for each agent to maintain an elite group of four leaders: on the first call, the group is populated with the best individuals from the initial population; on subsequent calls, it is updated if an individual better than the current leaders is found. Leaders store the best positions found
throughout the run
, not the best positions in the current population.
There is no rollback (greedy acceptance) here — the population moves freely, and this is a deliberate choice: this is the reference version, with no additions on top of the original mechanics.

InsertLeader inserts an agent into a list of four leaders sorted in descending order of fitness. If an agent's fitness exceeds that of any of the leaders, the position found determines the insertion point, the tail of the list shifts downward, and the agent takes its place. Since the leaders are not reset between iterations, the set of four solutions accumulated in this way always reflects the four best solutions encountered since the start of the run.

Conclusions
In its continuous form, BChimp is a mid-tier algorithm compared with other metaheuristics. After correcting the inherited coefficient bias, it scores 33.94% on the standard set of test functions, performing particularly poorly on Forest and losing ground as dimensionality increases: what performs decently with 10 coordinates falls apart at 1,000. The chaotic replacement phase, inherited from the original ChOA and intended as a mechanism for escaping local optima, proved more detrimental than beneficial to convergence in continuous optimization, so it is omitted from our implementation — the hunting phase alone, with a symmetric coefficient, is more stable.
The main value of the analysis lies not in the scores themselves, but in what was revealed along the way. First, the published form of the coefficient A has a sign bias (E[A] = f·(c1g − 1) ≠ 0). This goes unnoticed in a binary problem because the sigmoid transfer function masks both the sign and the step size — but in the continuous version, this bias drives the entire population into a corner of the search space. A clear lesson: a defect hidden behind binarization surfaces when the algorithm is ported to another domain, and copying the code verbatim from a publication results in an optimizer that does not work. Second, comparing the code with the publication and the original ChOA revealed a series of discrepancies — from mix-ups in the coefficient formulas to the questionable replacement phase. Third, a run on the Ackley function revealed the algorithm’s bias toward the coordinate origin: the nearly perfect result there is not a search achievement, but a coincidence between the algorithm’s structural attractor and the position of the optimum at the center of the symmetric range.
It is hard to recommend BChimp as a general-purpose optimizer. The ranking includes much stronger algorithms at the same computational cost. Its real niche, if any, is in low-dimensional problems or as a component of a hybrid approach. For serious high-dimensional optimization, it is neither a first nor a second choice.
For a trader optimizing an expert advisor’s parameters, entry thresholds, or money management rules, the conclusion is simple: a tool should be chosen based on its actual effectiveness in a complex, multidimensional landscape. The parameter space of a trading system is typically rugged and not centered around zero — precisely the conditions in which BChimp is weak and its bias toward the center works against the search.
A striking result may turn out to be an artifact of the test geometry rather than a genuine advantage — just as the ideal result for the Ackley function arose from the coincidence of the optimum with the center of the space. The discipline that protects against both pitfalls is the same: test under shifted, challenging, and out-of-sample conditions, rather than conditions known in advance to yield flattering results.
What stays with the reader, regardless of the fate of BChimp itself, is the habit of not trusting a source blindly. A published algorithm, just like someone else's strategy, may contain errors in its formulas, discrepancies, and hidden biases. Checking against the original source, analyzing the algorithm equation by equation, and benchmarking it honestly separate what works from what is merely attractively described.

for: The coefficient A has a sign bias (E[A] = f·(c1g − 1) ≠ 0), which drives the population into a corner in continuous search — this is a concrete, quantifiable defect tied to a formula and testable via trajectory analysis on historical runs

The symmetric correction A_k = f·C1G_k·(2·rand − 1) with E[A_k] = 0 is explicitly implemented and validated by comparing pre- and post-correction behavior on Hilly/Forest/Megacity functions across dimensionalities (5/25/500)

The chaotic replacement phase (50% probability jump via logistic map) is omitted because it proved 'detrimental to convergence' in continuous optimization — this decision is empirically grounded in observed degradation on standard test functions

The algorithm’s bias toward the coordinate origin is revealed on Ackley function, where 'nearly perfect result [...] is not a search achievement, but a coincidence between the algorithm’s structural attractor and the position of the optimum at the center' — directly testable via shifted Ackley variants

non_fatal: The article describes a population-based optimization algorithm (ChOA/BChimp) for continuous numerical optimization — not a trading signal or rule for financial markets.
No entry/exit conditions, stop levels, timeframes, asset-specific logic, or any element of a trading strategy are defined or implied.
The algorithm operates on abstract test functions (Hilly, Forest, Megacity, Ackley), not price/time series data.
There is no mapping from optimization variables to trading parameters (e.g., SL/TP, lot size, indicator thresholds) — the 'parameter space' discussed is generic and mathematical.

The conclusion explicitly states it is *not recommended* as a general-purpose optimizer, especially for high-dimensional, rugged, non-centered spaces — which matches typical trading parameter optimization scenarios.

The chaotic component, leader selection, averaging, and coefficient dynamics are all designed for global search in bounded Euclidean space — not for causal, real-time, sequential decision-making under market uncertainty.

judge.reject_reason: Статья описывает алгоритм глобальной оптимизации (Chimp Optimization Algorithm) для непрерывных численных задач, а не торговое правило. В тексте отсутствуют: условие входа (направление и параметры для long/short), таймфреймы, валютные пары, правила выхода или стоп-уровней, любая привязка к ценовым рядам или рыночным данным. Алгоритм работает с абстрактными тестовыми функциями (Hilly, Forest, Megacity), а не с OHLC-данными. Автор прямо указывает, что это не торговая стратегия, а инструмент оптимизации параметров, и даже предостерегает против его применения в торговых системах из-за слабой производительности в многомерных, нецентральных, шероховатых пространствах — что характерно для реальных торговых параметров. Следовательно, невозможно составить детерминированное правило для проверки на закрытых барах спот-форекса.
judge.summary: Статья представляет собой техническое описание и исправление метаэвристического алгоритма оптимизации ChOA/BChimp для решения непрерывных математических задач. Автор анализирует его поведение на стандартных тестовых функциях, выявляет и устраняет коэффициентный сдвиг, приводящий к дрейфу в угол поискового пространства, и демонстрирует результаты тестирования в виде процентных показателей эффективности относительно эталонных алгоритмов.
